explanation: Joshua 18:11 states: 'The lot of the tribe of Benjamin according to its clans came up.' (1) Dan was also among the seven tribes to receive a portion in a later chapter but was not the first tribe to draw the lot (near_passage). (2) Simeon received a portion within Judah's territory but was not the first tribe to draw the lot here (near_passage). (3) Issachar was also among the remaining tribes but did not draw the lot first (wrong_detail).

content: The daughters of Zelophehad came before Eleazar, Joshua, and the leaders to request what for themselves?
options: To be exempted from military service because their family had no male heir
To receive an inheritance among their father's brothers, since their father had no sons
To receive a fortified city as a place of refuge for their entire clan
To take their father's place and serve as priests at the Tent of Meeting at Shiloh
explanation: Joshua 17:3-4 states that Zelophehad had no sons, only daughters; they appealed to the LORD's command given to Moses and asked to receive an inheritance among their father's brothers, and Joshua granted it to them. (1) 'Exemption from military service' misrepresents their request; they sought the right to inherit land, not an exemption (wrong_detail) — this option is superficially plausible since it also concerns the absence of male heirs. (2) 'A fortified city as a place of refuge' confuses their request with the cities of refuge system described in another chapter (wrong_scope). (3) 'Serving as priests' is out of scope: the priesthood belonged to the line of Aaron and had no bearing on a request for a land inheritance (wrong_scope).

content: According to the text, why could the descendants of Manasseh not drive the Canaanites out of cities such as Beth-shean and Taanach?
options: Because the Canaanites were determined to remain, so Israel eventually only subjected them to forced labor rather than driving them out completely
Because the LORD had commanded that the Canaanites remain in the land in order to test Israel
Because the descendants of Manasseh had proactively made a peace covenant with the inhabitants of those cities
Because those cities actually lay outside the territory that had been allotted to Manasseh by lot
explanation: Joshua 17:12-13 records that the people of Manasseh could not take possession of those cities because the Canaanites were determined to remain in the land; later, when Israel grew strong, they subjected the Canaanites to forced labor but did not drive them out completely. (1) 'To test Israel' is the interpretation that appears in the book of Judges, not the reason stated in this passage (near_passage) — this option is close because it also speaks of Canaanites remaining. (2) 'Making a peace covenant' contradicts the text: they subjected them to forced labor rather than entering into a covenant (wrong_detail). (3) 'Outside Manasseh's territory' is incorrect: those cities belonged to Manasseh's allotted territory but could not be captured (wrong_detail).

content: When the descendants of Joseph complained that the hill country was not enough for them, what obstacle did they cite to justify their inability to take the lowland?
options: The Canaanites in the lowland were as numerous as the sand of the sea
The giant Anakim occupied the lowland
The Canaanites in the lowland had iron chariots
The cities of the lowland had fortified walls reaching to heaven
explanation: Joshua 17:16 records that the descendants of Joseph said that the Canaanites dwelling in the lowland — both in Beth-shean and in the Valley of Jezreel — all had iron chariots. (1) 'As numerous as the sand of the sea' is a description of the enemy used in other battles, not the reason cited here (near_passage). (2) 'The giant Anakim' relates to Caleb's hill country around Hebron, not the obstacle in the lowland mentioned in this verse (wrong_scope). (3) 'Walls reaching to heaven' comes from the negative spy report in Numbers/Deuteronomy, not from this passage (near_passage).

content: What question did Joshua use to rebuke the remaining seven tribes in order to urge them to go and take possession of the land?
options: Why are you afraid and do not dare to enter the land?
Why do you complain as you did in the wilderness before?
Who among you dares to rise up and lead the people to take possession of the land?
How long will you put off going to take possession of the land that the LORD has given you?
explanation: Joshua 18:3 records Joshua asking: 'How long will you put off going in to take possession of the land, which the LORD, the God of your fathers, has given you?' (1) 'Why are you afraid' is not the rebuke here; the text emphasizes delay, not fear (wrong_detail) — close because it is also a word of urging. (2) 'Complaining as in the wilderness' evokes events from the book of Numbers, not what Joshua said at Shiloh (near_passage). (3) 'Who dares to rise up and lead the people' misplaces the emphasis: the issue is collective delay, not a lack of leadership (wrong_detail).

content: According to the description of Benjamin's territorial boundary, how was this tribe's geographic position determined in relation to the two neighboring major tribes?
options: Located between the descendants of Judah to the north and the descendants of Joseph to the south
Located between the descendants of Judah to the south and the descendants of Joseph to the north
Located between the descendants of Simeon to the south and the descendants of Ephraim to the north
Located east of the Jordan River, bordering the descendants of Reuben and Gad
explanation: Joshua 18:11 records that the lot for Benjamin fell between the descendants of Judah and the descendants of Joseph, with its northern boundary bordering Joseph (Ephraim) and its southern boundary bordering Judah. (1) The option reversing the directions (Judah to the north, Joseph to the south) is wrong because Judah is to the south and Joseph is to the north (wrong_detail) — close because it names the correct two tribes but reverses the directions. (2) Replacing Judah with Simeon: although Simeon received its portion within Judah's territory, Benjamin's boundary is described in relation to Judah and Joseph, not Simeon (near_passage) — close because Simeon is associated with the region of Judah. (3) 'East of the Jordan bordering Reuben and Gad' is entirely out of scope: those are the tribes that received land on the other side of the river, while Benjamin is to the west (wrong_scope).

content: When the descendants of Joseph complained that they had received only one allotment despite being a numerous people, how did Joshua respond?
options: Told them to go up into the forest and clear the hill country for themselves, promising they would drive out the Canaanites even though they had iron chariots
Immediately granted them a second allotment in the fertile western plains
Commanded that a portion of Judah's land be transferred to them to make up what was lacking
Allowed them to temporarily postpone taking the land until they were strong enough to face the iron chariots
explanation: Joshua 17:15,17-18 records Joshua telling them that if they were a numerous people, they should go up to the forest and clear land in the territory of the Perizzites and the Rephaim, and assured them they would drive out the Canaanites even though they were powerful and had iron chariots. (1) 'Granting a second allotment' contradicts the answer: Joshua told them to expand by their own effort, not by giving another lot (wrong_detail) — close because it also addresses the issue of insufficient land. (2) 'Transferring land from Judah' is not in the text; the solution was to clear the forested area, not to take land from another tribe (wrong_detail) — close because it is also a way of expanding land. (3) 'Allowing them to postpone taking the land' is entirely contrary to the spirit of Joshua's answer, for Joshua urged them to advance immediately with a promise of victory (true_but_off — iron chariots are real in the passage but do not lead to this conclusion).
tags: Joshua's Reply to the Descendants of Joseph

content: In the second round of land allotment at Shiloh, which tribe received an inheritance that lay within the inheritance of the descendants of Judah?
options: Simeon
Zebulun
Issachar
Dan
explanation: Joshua 19:1 records that the second lot fell to the tribe of Simeon, and their inheritance was within the inheritance of the descendants of Judah. Zebulun (wrong_detail) received the third lot and its land was in the north, not within Judah. Issachar (wrong_detail) received the fourth lot, in the region of the Valley of Jezreel. Dan (wrong_scope) was the tribe that received its lot last and had to go conquer Leshem in the far north.
tags: Division of Land Among the Tribes

content: After the tribes had finished dividing the land, the people of Israel gave Joshua his own city as an inheritance, at the command of the LORD. What city was it?
options: Timnath-serah
Hebron
Shiloh
Shechem
explanation: Joshua 19:49-50 records that they gave Joshua the city of Timnath-serah in the hill country of Ephraim, at the command of the LORD. Hebron (wrong_detail) was the city given to Caleb, not Joshua. Shiloh (near_passage) was where the tabernacle was set up and the lot-casting for the land division took place, not Joshua's personal inheritance. Shechem (wrong_scope) later became a city of refuge but was not the reward given to Joshua.

content: The LORD commanded Joshua to establish cities of refuge in order to protect which category of people?
options: A manslayer fleeing from the avenger of blood
Levites who had no inheritance of land
Foreigners and resident aliens in the land
Debtors unable to repay their creditors
explanation: Joshua 20:2–3 records that the cities of refuge were for anyone who kills a person unintentionally, without premeditation, to flee from the avenger of blood. The Levites (near_passage) did indeed have no inheritance, but that is the subject of chapter 21, not the purpose of the cities of refuge. Foreigners and resident aliens (wrong_detail) are mentioned in verse 9 as also enjoying the right of refuge, but they are not the primary intended group. Debtors (common_misconception) belong to the law of the Year of Jubilee and have no connection to the cities of refuge.

content: Because their allotted territory was too small, the descendants of the tribe of Dan went up and captured a distant city, then renamed it after their ancestor. What was that city originally called?
options: Laish
Ashkelon
Gaza
Ashdod
explanation: Joshua 19:47 records that the descendants of Dan went and fought against Laish, captured it, and called it Dan after the name of their ancestor. Ashkelon (wrong_scope), Gaza, and Ashdod (wrong_scope) are all cities of the Philistines on the coastal plain, not the place where Dan relocated to in the far north.

content: When listing the inheritance of the tribe of Zebulun, the text mentions Bethlehem among their cities. Why is this detail likely to confuse readers?
options: Because there is a northern Bethlehem distinct from the famous Bethlehem of Judah
Because Bethlehem originally belonged to the inheritance of Issachar, not Zebulun
Because Bethlehem was where the tabernacle was set up before being moved to Shiloh
Because Bethlehem is one of the cities of refuge established in chapter 20
explanation: Joshua 19:15 lists Bethlehem within Zebulun's northern territory; this is a different Bethlehem from the Bethlehem of Judah, the hometown of David, which is why it is easily confused. The option that Bethlehem belonged to Issachar (wrong_detail) is incorrect because the text places it within Zebulun's allotment (19:10–15). The tabernacle at Bethlehem (wrong_detail) is incorrect because the tabernacle was erected at Shiloh (Joshua 18:1). Bethlehem as a city of refuge (wrong_scope) is incorrect because the cities of refuge named in 20:7–8 do not include Bethlehem.

content: According to the law of the cities of refuge, when a manslayer fled to the gate of a city, what must the elders do first in order for that person to receive asylum?
options: Hear that person's account of the matter and then receive him into the city to dwell with them
Immediately bring that person before the whole congregation for trial
Hand that person over to the avenger of blood to decide his fate
Require that person to remain outside the gate until the high priest dies
explanation: Joshua 20:4 records that the one who flees must state his case in the hearing of the elders at the gate of the city, and they shall take him into the city and give him a place to dwell among them. Bringing him before the congregation for trial (true_but_off) does indeed occur (verse 6), but it takes place after he has already been received — it is not the first step. Handing him over to the avenger of blood (common_misconception) contradicts the entire protective purpose of the city. Requiring him to remain outside the gate until the high priest dies (wrong_detail) confuses the condition for returning home (verse 6) with the initial reception procedure.

content: The six cities of refuge were distributed equally on both sides of the Jordan River. Which pair of cities listed below were BOTH located on the WEST side of the Jordan?
options: Kedesh and Hebron
Bezer and Ramoth
Golan and Shechem
Ramoth and Hebron
explanation: Joshua 20:7 records that the three cities on the west side of the Jordan were Kedesh in Galilee, Shechem in the hill country of Ephraim, and Kirjath-arba (that is, Hebron) in the hill country of Judah; so Kedesh and Hebron are both on the west side. Bezer and Ramoth (wrong_detail) are both eastern cities (verse 8). Golan and Shechem (wrong_detail) pair an eastern city, Golan, with a western city, Shechem, so they are not on the same side. Ramoth and Hebron (wrong_detail) likewise pair an eastern city with a western city.

content: Where was the casting of lots for the remaining tribes' inheritance carried out, and who presided over it?
options: At Shiloh before the entrance of the tent of meeting, by Eleazar the priest and Joshua together with the heads of the families
At Gilgal where they first camped, presided over by Joshua alone
At Shechem by Mount Gerizim, by Eleazar and the Levitical priests
At Hebron, the city of Caleb, by Joshua and twelve family heads
explanation: Joshua 19:51 records that Eleazar, Joshua, and the heads of the families cast lots for the inheritance at Shiloh, before the entrance of the tent of meeting. Gilgal with Joshua alone (wrong_detail) is wrong in both location and leadership, since Eleazar the priest was also present. Shechem by Gerizim (wrong_scope) was the site of a later covenant ceremony, not the casting of lots. Hebron, the city of Caleb (true_but_off) is indeed Caleb's inheritance, but it was not where the tent of meeting stood for the distribution of the land.

content: A man who had committed accidental manslaughter was received into a city of refuge. According to the law, when was he permitted to leave the city and return to his own home without fear of the avenger of blood?
options: When the high priest who was serving at the time died
After he had stayed in the city of refuge for a full seven years
When the congregation had judged him and declared him innocent
When the avenger of blood had died or withdrew his claim
explanation: Joshua 20:6 states that the manslayer must remain in the city of refuge until the death of the high priest who was in office at the time, after which he could return to his own home. Staying a full seven years (wrong_detail) confuses this with other legal timeframes such as the Sabbath year; the text does not mention a seven-year period. The congregation judging and declaring him innocent (true_but_off) is the step for being admitted to the city and confirmed as a manslayer, not the condition for returning home. The avenger of blood dying or withdrawing his claim (common_misconception) sounds plausible, but the law specifies only one condition for return: the death of the high priest.

content: Unlike the other tribes, each of which received a distinct territorial boundary, what was unique about Simeon's inheritance, and what reason does the text give?
options: It was located within the territory of Judah, because Judah's portion was too large for their needs
It was situated along the western coast, because Judah ceded its coastal region to Simeon
It stretched on both sides of the Jordan River, because Simeon was more populous than the other tribes
It consisted of towns scattered among multiple tribes, because Simeon was cursed to be dispersed
explanation: Joshua 19:1 and 19:9 record that Simeon's inheritance was taken from within the territory of Judah, because the portion of the descendants of Judah was too large for them, so Simeon received their inheritance within Judah's territory. Situated along the coast because Judah ceded its coastal region (wrong_detail) is incorrect, since the reason the text gives is that Judah's portion was too large, not that they surrendered the coastline. Stretching on both sides of the Jordan because of a larger population (wrong_detail) is incorrect; that was the situation of Reuben, Gad, and the half-tribe of Manasseh. Scattered towns because of a curse of dispersion (true_but_off) accords with Jacob's prophecy in Genesis, but chapter 19 explains the arrangement solely in terms of Judah's territory being too large.

content: According to Joshua 21, what did the Israelites give to the Levites so that they could live among the tribes?
options: Cities and the pasturelands surrounding them
A tithe of the produce from every harvest season
A contiguous strip of land in the southern part of the territory
The firstborn of their livestock
explanation: Joshua 21:3 records that the Israelites, as commanded by the LORD, gave the Levites from their own inheritance cities and their pasturelands. The option 'a tithe of the produce' confuses this with the tithe system for Levites found in other legal passages — it is not what Joshua 21 describes (wrong_scope). 'A contiguous strip of land' is incorrect because the Levites did not receive a continuous territorial allotment but rather scattered cities (wrong_detail). 'The firstborn of the livestock' belongs to the offerings presented to the priests and is not the content of the city distribution (wrong_scope).

content: According to Joshua 21, how many cities in total were given to the Levites within the inheritance of the Israelites?
options: Twenty-four cities
Thirty-six cities
Forty-eight cities
Sixty cities
explanation: Joshua 21:41 states that all the cities of the Levites within the inheritance of the Israelites totaled forty-eight cities with their pasturelands. 'Twenty-four' and 'thirty-six' are incorrect figures that do not match the total given in the text (wrong_detail). 'Sixty cities' recalls the sixty cities of the region of Argob found elsewhere in Scripture but is not the number of Levitical cities here (near_passage).

content: When lots were cast to distribute cities among the Levites, from which tribes did the Kohathite clan who were descendants of Aaron (the priests) first receive cities?
options: From the tribes of Judah, Simeon, and Benjamin
From the tribes of Ephraim, Dan, and the half-tribe of Manasseh
From the tribes of Issachar, Asher, and Naphtali
From the tribes of Reuben, Gad, and Zebulun
explanation: Joshua 21:4 records that the lot fell for the Kohathite families; the descendants of the priest Aaron received thirteen cities from the tribes of Judah, Simeon, and Benjamin — the region near the future temple. The option 'Ephraim, Dan, and the half-tribe of Manasseh' was the portion given to the rest of the Kohathite clan, not the Aaronic branch (almost-right, wrong_detail). Issachar, Asher, and Naphtali are the tribes that allotted cities to the Gershonite clan (wrong_scope). Reuben and Gad belong to the group that gave cities to the Merarite clan (wrong_scope).

content: At the end of chapter 21, why does the author emphasize that 'not one word of all the good promises that the LORD had made to the house of Israel had failed'?
options: To confirm that God had completely kept all His promises to give the land and rest to the people
To warn the people that there were still many enemies they needed to drive out
To explain why the people had to continue wandering in the wilderness
To remind the people that the covenant would only be fulfilled when a king was established
explanation: Joshua 21:43-45 records that the LORD gave to Israel all the land He had sworn to give to their fathers, gave them rest on every side, and not one word of all His good promises had failed — all came to pass. The option 'there were still many enemies' contradicts verse 44, which says the LORD gave all their enemies into their hands (almost-right, wrong_detail). 'Continue wandering in the wilderness' belongs to the period before Joshua, contrary to the context of having already entered the promised land (wrong_scope). 'When a king was established' did not occur until the time of Samuel and has no connection to the promise about the land here (common_misconception).

content: At the beginning of chapter 22, what did Joshua do with the tribes of Reuben, Gad, and the half-tribe of Manasseh after the land had been conquered?
options: Blessed them and sent them back to their own camps on the other side of the Jordan
Appointed them as guardians of the Ark of the Covenant
Punished them for being unfaithful during the war
Sent them to continue fighting the peoples in the north
explanation: Joshua 22:6 records that Joshua blessed them and sent them away, and they returned to their own camps on the other (eastern) side of the Jordan after having helped their brothers conquer the land. 'Guarding the Ark of the Covenant' was the duty of the Levites, not this group (wrong_scope). 'Punished for unfaithfulness' is the exact opposite of the text, since Joshua commended them for keeping the word of Moses (wrong_detail). 'Sent to fight in the north' is incorrect because the campaign was complete and they were released to go home (wrong_detail).

content: When sending the eastern tribes home, what did Joshua instruct them to do with the great wealth, livestock, and plunder they were bringing back?
options: Divide the spoil taken from their enemies with their brothers
Dedicate everything to the storehouse of the tabernacle at Shiloh
Burn it all according to the ban of destruction applied to foreign peoples
Set it aside exclusively for the use of the priests of Aaron
explanation: Joshua 22:8 records that Joshua instructed them to return to their camps with much wealth, livestock, silver, gold, and clothing, and to divide the spoil of their enemies with their brothers. 'Dedicate everything to the storehouse at Shiloh' confuses this instruction with the regulations about plunder from Jericho found elsewhere (near_passage). 'Burn it all under the ban of destruction' applied to certain specific cities, not to spoil meant to be divided and taken home (wrong_scope). 'Set aside for the priests' is incorrect because the instruction was explicitly to share it with their brothers (wrong_detail).

content: When they heard news about the structure beside the Jordan that was suspected of being an act of rebellion, what did the congregation of Israel do BEFORE deciding to go to war?
options: Sent the priest Phinehas and ten chiefs to confront them
Immediately mobilized the entire army to attack the eastern tribes
Sought the will of the LORD by casting the Urim
Sent Joshua himself to go and tear down the structure
explanation: Joshua 22:13-14 records that they sent Phinehas, son of the priest Eleazar, together with ten chiefs representing the ten tribes to meet with the eastern tribes and investigate the matter. The option 'immediately mobilized the army to attack' is true that they assembled to go to war (v. 12), but the first action taken was to send a delegation to investigate (almost-right, wrong_detail). 'Casting the Urim' is not mentioned in the text in connection with this incident (common_misconception). 'Joshua himself going to tear it down' is incorrect because the one sent was Phinehas, not Joshua (wrong_detail).

content: What was the true reason that the tribes of Reuben, Gad, and the half-tribe of Manasseh gave for building the structure beside the Jordan River?
options: As a witness so that the descendants of both sides would know they share in the worship of the LORD
To offer burnt offerings and peace offerings there in place of the tabernacle
To mark the boundary of the land that Moses had given them in former times
To show repentance for sins they had committed during their joint campaigns
explanation: Joshua 22:24-28 records that they built the structure as a witness, lest in future days the descendants of the western tribes say that the eastern descendants have no share in the LORD; it serves as a witness that they worship Him together, not as a place to offer sacrifices. The option 'to offer burnt offerings in place of the tabernacle' is precisely what they denied (v.26, almost-right, wrong_detail). 'To mark the land boundary' is not the purpose the text states (wrong_scope). 'To show repentance for sins during the campaigns' is fabricated and not found in their explanation (common_misconception).

content: In their rebuke, which two past events did the Israelite delegation cite to warn that the sin of a few could bring disaster upon the entire congregation?
options: The sin at Peor and Achan's sin concerning the devoted things
The sin at Peor and the rebellion of Korah
The worship of the golden calf and Achan's sin concerning the devoted things
The rebellion of Korah and the worship of the golden calf
explanation: Joshua 22:17 references 'the iniquity of Peor' (Numbers 25, a plague that fell on the congregation) and v.20 references 'Achan the son of Zerah, who broke faith in the matter of the devoted things,' causing God's wrath to fall on the whole congregation — these are exactly the two events cited. The option 'Peor and the rebellion of Korah' is correct about Peor but Korah is not cited here (almost-right, wrong_detail). 'The golden calf and Achan' is correct about Achan but substitutes the golden calf for Peor, which is not mentioned in the passage (almost-right, wrong_detail). 'Korah and the golden calf' is wrong on both counts as neither matches the two events the text cites (wrong_scope).

content: After hearing the explanation, how did Phinehas and the leaders respond, and what model of conflict resolution does this demonstrate?
options: They were satisfied, acknowledged that the LORD was in their midst, and abandoned their intention to go to war
They remained suspicious and required the structure to be demolished before they would withdraw
They demanded that the eastern tribes pay a fine before granting forgiveness
They withdrew in silence but reported back so the congregation could decide later
explanation: Joshua 22:30-33 records that the words of the eastern tribes pleased Phinehas and the leaders; he said 'today we know that the LORD is in our midst' because they had not committed this breach of faith, so the congregation abandoned their intention to go to war and praised God. This is a model for conflict resolution: investigate, listen, then reconcile. 'Remained suspicious and demolished the structure' contradicts the text since the structure was kept as a witness (v.34, almost-right, wrong_detail). 'Demanded a fine before forgiving' does not appear in the recorded response (common_misconception). 'Withdrew in silence for the congregation to decide later' is wrong since the matter was resolved and they rejoiced on the spot (almost-right, wrong_detail).

content: When Joshua summoned the people of Israel to deliver his farewell address, how was his condition described?
options: He was old and advanced in years
He was seriously ill
He had just won a great battle
He was about to set out to war
explanation: Joshua 23:1-2 records that Joshua was old and advanced in years, so he summoned all Israel along with the elders to give his charge. 'Seriously ill' is an incorrect detail; the text does not say he was sick (wrong_detail). 'Had just won a great battle' confuses this with the earlier conquest period — by this time the wars had ceased (near_passage). 'About to set out to war' contradicts the context that the land had already been given rest (wrong_scope).

content: At what location did Joshua gather all the tribes of Israel to make the final covenant?
options: Shechem
Shiloh
Gilgal
Jericho
explanation: Joshua 24:1 records that Joshua assembled all the tribes at Shechem and they presented themselves before God. 'Shiloh' was where the tabernacle had previously been set up, making it easy to confuse (near_passage). 'Gilgal' was where they camped when they first entered the promised land (near_passage). 'Jericho' was the first city captured, not the place where the covenant was made (wrong_scope).

content: In Joshua's historical review, where did he say the forefather Abraham originally lived before God brought him through the land of Canaan?
options: Beyond the River
In the land of Egypt
In the wilderness of Sinai
At Mount Seir
explanation: Joshua 24:2–3 records that your fathers, including Terah the father of Abraham, lived beyond the River (the Euphrates) and served other gods; then God brought Abraham across. 'In the land of Egypt' is where the people lived later, in Jacob's time (near_passage). 'The wilderness of Sinai' comes at a later stage, after the exodus from Egypt (wrong_scope). 'Mount Seir' is the region God gave to Esau and has nothing to do with Abraham's origin (wrong_detail).

content: According to the closing section of the book of Joshua, how old was Joshua when he died?
options: One hundred and ten years old
One hundred and twenty years old
One hundred and thirty years old
Ninety years old
explanation: Joshua 24:29 records that Joshua the servant of the LORD died at the age of one hundred and ten years. 'One hundred and twenty years old' is the age at which Moses died, making it an easy mix-up (common_misconception). 'One hundred and thirty years old' is simply the wrong number (wrong_detail). 'Ninety years old' is also incorrect for Joshua's age at death (wrong_detail).

content: Joshua declared that one Israelite could put a thousand enemies to flight. What reason did he give to explain this extraordinary power?
options: The LORD their God was fighting for them
Because their weapons were superior
Because those nations were already weakened
Because of the oath of loyalty among the tribes
explanation: Joshua 23:10 records, 'One man of you puts to flight a thousand, since it is the LORD your God who fights for you, just as he promised you.' The emphasis is entirely on God fighting, not human strength. 'Because their weapons were superior' is a purely military explanation that misses the theological point (true_but_off). 'Because those nations were already weakened' sounds plausible but the text does not say this — it attributes the power to God's action (wrong_detail). 'Because of the oath of loyalty among the tribes' conflates this with the covenant renewal scene and is not the stated reason for military strength (near_passage).

content: Joshua warned that if the Israelites intermarried with the remaining nations, what consequence would they face?
options: Those nations would become a snare and a scourge, and Israel would lose the good land
They would be immediately exiled beyond the River
God would remove the Ark of the Covenant from their midst
They would be forced to pay heavy tribute to those nations
explanation: Joshua 23:12–13 warns that if Israel intermarries with the remaining nations, those peoples will become 'a snare and a trap for you, a whip on your sides and thorns in your eyes, until you perish from off this good ground.' 'Exiled beyond the River' borrows imagery from where the fathers originated in chapter 24 but is outside the scope of this passage (near_passage). 'God removing the Ark of the Covenant' is a consequence not mentioned here at all (wrong_detail). 'Being forced to pay heavy tribute' sounds plausible but is absent from the text; the stated consequence is loss of the land (wrong_detail).

content: When recalling how the king of Moab hired Balaam to deal with Israel, what did Joshua say God caused to happen?
options: Balaam kept blessing Israel instead of cursing them
Balaam was struck mute and could not say a word
The king of Moab changed his mind and made a peace treaty
Balaam's donkey turned around and bit him
explanation: Joshua 24:9–10 records that Balak sent and called Balaam to curse Israel, but God would not listen to Balaam, so he blessed Israel repeatedly, and God delivered them from Balak's hand. 'Balaam was struck mute' is incorrect in detail; he still spoke, but what he spoke was blessing, not cursing (wrong_detail). 'The king of Moab changed his mind and made a peace treaty' has no basis in the text (wrong_detail). 'Balaam's donkey turning and biting him' mixes in the narrative of the donkey speaking from Numbers, which is outside the scope of this passage and factually wrong here (near_passage).

content: After the people committed to keeping the covenant, Joshua set up a witness object and explained its significance — what did he say about it?
options: A large stone as a witness because it had heard all the words the LORD had spoken
An altar of stone on which to offer burnt offerings to the LORD
A bronze pillar engraved with the commandments of the covenant
A pile of stones commemorating the crossing of the Jordan River
explanation: Joshua 24:26-27 records that Joshua took a large stone and set it up under the terebinth by the sanctuary of the LORD, declaring that the stone would serve as a witness because it had heard all the words the LORD had spoken. 'An altar to offer burnt offerings' changes the function of the object that was set up — this was a witness stone, not a sacrificial altar (wrong_detail). 'A bronze pillar engraved with commandments' is wrong in both material and description (wrong_detail). 'A pile of stones commemorating the crossing of the Jordan' refers to the twelve stones in chapter 4, which is a different passage (near_passage).

content: When the people eagerly vowed to serve the LORD, Joshua responded with what seemed like a paradox — what was his argument meant to emphasize?
options: God is holy and jealous, and will not tolerate half-hearted or unfaithful commitment
The people were not yet mature enough to bear the responsibilities of the covenant
They must first offer a sin offering before being permitted to take such a vow
Only the elders had the authority to make a covenant on behalf of the people
explanation: Joshua 24:19-20 records Joshua saying, 'You are not able to serve the LORD, for he is a holy God. He is a jealous God; he will not forgive your transgressions or your sins. If you forsake the LORD and serve foreign gods, then he will turn and do you harm.' The purpose is to warn the people against making a superficial commitment, because God is holy and jealous. 'They were not yet mature enough to bear the responsibility' fabricates a reason not found in the text — the passage speaks about God's nature, not the people's age (wrong_detail). 'They must first offer a sin offering before making a vow' sounds religiously plausible but is not the argument being made here (true_but_off). 'Only the elders may make the covenant on behalf of the people' contradicts the fact that all the people responded and committed together (wrong_scope).

content: In his review of Israel's history, what foundational truth did Joshua emphasize to help the people understand why they must faithfully serve God?
options: They were enjoying land, cities, and orchards they had not labored to build or plant themselves
They had personally defeated all the Canaanite peoples with their own swords and bows
They had kept the law completely throughout their wilderness journey
They were promised additional land beyond the great river if they remained obedient
explanation: Joshua 24:13 records: 'I gave you a land on which you had not labored and cities that you had not built, and you dwell in them. You eat the fruit of vineyards and olive orchards that you did not plant' — the foundation for faithfulness is God's unearned grace. 'They personally defeated all the peoples with their swords and bows' directly contradicts 24:12, which states it was not by their sword or bow (common_misconception, almost-right since it is adjacent to the passage in question). 'They kept the law completely throughout the wilderness' has a pious ring but is not the reason stated here, and contradicts the actual record of their wilderness journey (true_but_off). 'They were promised additional land beyond the great river if they obeyed' invents a promise not found in the text, confusing this with the mention of the forefathers' origins in 24:2-3 (near_passage).
